turns.prompt_text: I have a bunch of beeswax that I poured into a half gallon of milk container While the wax floated to the top and the water separated on bottom, so now it's more like the top third of that half gallon of milk The problem that it ran into is that the dirt and sediment also Rose to the top of the water and rested at the bottom of the wax Because of this, it's kind of tough to scrape it because it's at the thickest layer I feel like I should have turned it upside down so that all of the dirt and sediment went in rests at that position between the two layers would have been in a tight and narrow area that I could have cleanly cut off with a knife So essentially I need to build an hourglass out of two different milk jugs The problem that I then run into is that I need to balance it so that the boundary between water and beeswax is near perfectly to that Central axiom One method of control that I have power over is in adding more water so I can raise the wax up I guess technically I could also lower the water if I introduce some kind of spout at the bottom so that I can fully control how much water is in the bottom part
turns.response_html:
What you're describing is the exact mechanism of a separatory funnel—a classic piece of chemistry glassware designed to drain away a heavier bottom liquid (water) to isolate a lighter top liquid (wax).

Your instinct to control the water volume to dictate exactly where the sediment layer lands is spot on. Here are two ways to engineer your way out of this:

1. The Bottom Drain (Separatory Funnel Method)

Adding a spout at the bottom is the cleanest mechanical solution. Instead of trying to perfectly balance the water level so the sediment lands in a narrow neck, you just drain the water out completely until the dirt line drops down to the exit point.

You can modify a single milk jug by tapping the bottom with a 1/4-inch inner diameter hose barb fitting. Attach a short length of tubing and a simple inline valve. While the wax is still liquid but separating, open the valve. The water drains out, and the sediment layer drops straight down to the narrowest point at the bottom, where it can be easily flushed out or cut away once hardened.

2. The Custom Hourglass Coupler

If you want to stick to the hourglass idea, trying to tape or glue two jugs together will likely leak when introduced to hot water.

You can model a custom threaded coupler and print it on your Bambu Lab A1. The print would feature two female threads matching the milk jug pitch, with a narrow central aperture serving as the choke point. Screw a jug into each side. You can then add water to the top jug to float the wax boundary exactly into the 3D-printed choke point. When the wax cools and solidifies, you simply unscrew the jugs, and the sediment is isolated in the narrow printed neck for a clean cut.

The Pre-Filtering Alternative

To avoid the sediment problem entirely on your next batch, you can prevent the "slumgum" (the dark mix of propolis, dirt, and cocoon remnants) from ever reaching the cooling container.

Next time you melt the comb, tie it up tightly in an old pair of pantyhose or a few layers of cheesecloth before submerging it in the hot water. The pure wax melts and floats through the mesh, while the sediment remains trapped in the bag. When the container cools, you're left with a perfectly clean disk of yellow wax floating on the water, with zero scraping required.

turns.prompt_text: Which of those two methods as well cost effective and more overall effective
turns.response_html:
Here is how the two custom setups stack up against each other:

1. The Bottom Drain (Separatory Funnel)

  • Cost-Effectiveness: High. You might already have a spare 1/4-inch inner diameter hose barb fitting and some tubing to tap the jug. Even if you need to pick up a plastic inline valve at a home improvement store, applying a 10% military discount keeps the entire project under five dollars.
  • Overall Effectiveness: Winner. This gives you absolute, real-time control over the separation. You don't have to guess liquid volumes; you simply watch the boundary layer drop and close the valve the exact second the sediment clears the drain.

2. The Custom Hourglass Coupler

  • Cost-Effectiveness: Winner. Designing and printing the threaded coupler on your Bambu Lab A1 costs mere pennies in filament and uses manufacturing tools you already have running.
  • Overall Effectiveness: Lower. Fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D prints naturally have microscopic layer lines that are prone to weeping liquids. When you introduce the thermal expansion and stress of hot water—which needs to reach at least 145°F to keep the beeswax melted—the risk of the threaded joints leaking increases significantly. Furthermore, perfectly calibrating the water volume to land the sediment exactly in the narrow choke point requires frustrating trial and error.

The Verdict

The Bottom Drain is the much better engineered solution. The precision control it offers far outweighs the minor hardware cost, and it completely bypasses the leaking risks of 3D-printed threads under thermal stress.

That said, the absolute most effective and cheapest method for your future batches is to avoid the separation problem entirely through pre-filtering. The standard practice for processing hive harvests is to tightly wrap the raw comb in a few layers of cheesecloth before submerging it in the boiling pot. The hot water melts the wax so it seeps through the mesh and floats to the top, while the dirt, cocoon remnants, and propolis remain physically trapped in the cloth. Once it cools, you simply pop out a perfectly clean disc of wax.
